body.objective: Students will be able to select and curate a portfolio.
body.iCan: I can select and curate a portfolio.
successCriteria: I can select works that show range and a strong personal voice
I can sequence and present a portfolio
I can document work with clear photos and labels
body.hook: A university portfolio reviewer may spend only a few minutes on your work. In that time they need to see who you are as an artist. Curating means choosing what to leave out as much as what to put in.

vocabulary.definition: A curated collection of an artist's best work.
To select and arrange works for a purpose and audience.
The order in which works are presented.
Photos and information that record an artwork.
Sketches and studies showing how an artwork developed.

study.title: Curate Your Best
study.question: How do artists choose and present their strongest work?
study.passage:
Part 1, Inventory (15 minutes): Lay out or list every artwork from Grades 10 to 12. Rate each from 1 to 4 on skill, idea and personal voice.
Part 2, Know the audience (5 minutes): Portfolios for art schools often ask for 10 to 20 works, mostly from observation plus some personal projects and sketchbook pages. Exhibitions need a theme and space plan.
Part 3, Select (15 minutes): Choose 12 works that show: drawing from observation, range of media, a series or theme, and at least two process pages. Remove weaker pieces even if they took a long time.
Part 4, Sequence (10 minutes): Start and end with your strongest works. Group related pieces.
Part 5, Document (15 minutes): Photograph each work square-on in even, natural light with no glare, cropped to the edges. Label: title, medium, size, year. Write one or two sentences per work.
study.source: Original studio task written for this lesson; portfolio guidance summarized from post-secondary art program requirements.
steps: Inventory and rate all your work
Identify the audience and its requirements
Select 12 works showing range and voice
discussion: Which work was hardest to leave out? Why?
Why open and close with your strongest work?
What does your portfolio say about you as an artist?
How does a poor photo affect how a reviewer sees good work?
study.product: Assemble a digital portfolio of 12 documented works with labels, sequence and a 150-word artist statement.

examples.title: Selection
examples.problem: You spent 20 hours on a weak painting. Include it?
examples.answer: No; include only works that show your best skill and voice
examples.explore: What could you do with it instead?

examples.title: Sequence
examples.problem: Where should your strongest work go?
examples.answer: First, with another strong work last
examples.explore: Why do the middle works matter less?

examples.title: Documentation
examples.problem: How do you photograph a painting?
examples.answer: Shoot straight on in indirect natural light and crop to the edges

practice.q: Name the four parts of an artwork label.

practice.a: Photos and information recording an artwork.

practice.q: How should you light a photo of artwork?
practice.a: Even, indirect natural light without glare.

practice.q: What three criteria help rate works?

practice.a: To show series and themes clearly.

practice.q: What do art schools often want to see?
practice.a: Observational drawing, range of media, personal projects.

practice.q: Why crop artwork photos to the edges?
Why should time spent not decide selection?
How does a portfolio show personal voice?
practice.a: Recurring themes, subjects and approaches across works.

practice.q: How would a portfolio for an exhibition differ from one for an art school?
practice.a: An exhibition follows a theme and space; a school portfolio shows range and skill.

practice.q: What should you do if two works are very similar?
practice.a: Choose the stronger one or present them as a series.

misconceptions: Including every artwork to show effort
Leaving out sketchbook and process work
exitTicket: Name three things a strong portfolio should show.
Write a label for one of your works.

items.q: Define portfolio.
items.answer: A curated collection of an artist's best work.

items.q: What are the parts of an artwork label?
items.answer: Title, medium, size, year.

items.q: Explain how to photograph a 2D artwork well.
items.answer: Straight on, even indirect light, no glare, cropped to edges.

items.q: Why should you start with your strongest work?
items.answer: First impressions shape how reviewers see the rest.

items.q: Name three things art schools often look for.
items.answer: Observational drawing, range of media, personal voice or process.

items.q: Why include process work?
items.answer: It shows thinking, development and problem-solving.

items.q: Explain how you would choose 12 works from 30.
items.answer: Rate on skill, idea and voice; keep range and series; remove weaker or repeated works.

items.q: Describe what your portfolio would say about you as an artist.
items.answer: Answers vary.
